facts.statement: Site S, located one kilometer southwest of the Tendaguru Hill, was the most important source of Giraffatitan fossils.

facts.statement: The initial description was based on specimens recovered from the Tendaguru formation between 1909 and 1912.
facts.quote: based on several specimens recovered between 1909 and 1912 from the Tendaguru formation

facts.statement: The species is known from five partial skeletons, three of which include skulls.
facts.quote: It is known from five partial skeletons, including three skulls

facts.statement: Giraffatitan lived between 145 and 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: It lived from 145 to 150 million years ago, during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic period

facts.statement: Skelett SII, a partial skeleton from Tendaguru, serves as the lectotype for Giraffatitan brancai.
facts.quote: The lectotype material of Giraffatitan brancai is skeleton "Skelett SII", a partial skeleton from Tendaguru

facts.statement: In 2009, Taylor selected Skelett SII as the lectotype because it was more complete.

facts.statement: Starting in 1909, Werner Janensch discovered many additional Giraffatitan specimens in Tanzania.
facts.quote: Beginning in 1909, Werner Janensch found many additional G. brancai specimens in Tanzania, Africa

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul suggested separating the species based on differences in vertebral proportions compared to B. altithorax.
facts.quote: In 1988 Gregory S. Paul published a new reconstruction of the skeleton of B. brancai, highlighting differences in proportion between it and B. altithorax

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul initially proposed separating the species only at the subgenus level rather than the genus level.
facts.quote: Paul believed that the limb and girdle elements of both species were very similar, and therefore suggested they be separated not at genus, but only at subgenus level

facts.statement: George Olshevsky elevated Giraffatitan to full genus status in 1991.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was raised to full genus level by George Olshevsky in 1991

facts.statement: Daniel Chure rejected the separation in 2010, but most subsequent studies from 2012 onwards accepted the name Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: The split was rejected by Daniel Chure in 2010, but from 2012 onward most studies recognized the name Giraffatitan

facts.statement: From 1914 until the 1990s, Giraffatitan was considered the largest known dinosaur.
facts.quote: Between 1914 and the 1990s, Giraffatitan was claimed to be the largest dinosaur known

facts.statement: Size estimates for Giraffatitan rely on the Berlin museum skeleton, which is partially made of authentic bones.
facts.quote: All size estimates for Giraffatitan are based on the skeleton mounted in Berlin, which is partly constructed from authentic bones

facts.statement: The Berlin mount is largely based on specimen HMN SII, a subadult measuring between 21.8 and 22.46 meters in length and approximately 12 meters tall.
facts.quote: These were largely taken from specimen HMN SII, a subadult individual between 21.8 - 22.46 m in length and about 12 m tall

facts.statement: Historical mass estimates for Giraffatitan have varied widely, ranging from 15 to 78 tonnes.
facts.quote: Mass estimates are more problematic and historically have strongly varied from as little as 15 t to as much as 78 t

facts.statement: In 1950, Janensch estimated the weight of the larger skeleton at forty tonnes.
facts.quote: In 1950, he mentioned a weight of forty tonnes for the larger skeleton

facts.statement: In 1980, Dale Alan Russell estimated a weight of 14.8 tonnes based on humerus and thighbone diameters.
facts.quote: In 1980, Dale Alan Russell et al published a much lower weight of 14.8 tonnes by extrapolating from the diameter of the humerus and the thighbone

facts.statement: In 2020, Molina-Perez and Larramnedi estimated HMN XV2 to be 25 meters long, 48 tonnes, with a shoulder height of 6.8 meters.
facts.quote: In 2020, Molina-Perez and Larramnedi estimated the size of the HMN XV2 specimen at 25 m and 48 t, with a shoulder height of 6.8 m

facts.statement: Giraffatitan was a four-legged, plant-eating sauropod dinosaur characterized by a long neck and tail.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was a sauropod, one of a group of four-legged, plant-eating dinosaurs with long necks and tails.

facts.statement: The tail of Giraffatitan made up approximately 27.2% of its total body length.
facts.quote: The estimated tail length makes up approximately 27.2% of the total body length.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan had a giraffe-like build featuring long forelimbs and a very long neck.
facts.quote: It had a giraffe-like build, with long forelimbs and a very long neck.

facts.statement: The skull of Giraffatitan featured a tall arch before the eyes, bony nares, other openings, and spatulate teeth resembling chisels.
facts.quote: The skull had a tall arch anterior to the eyes, consisting of the bony nares, a number of other openings, and "spatulate" teeth (resembling chisels).

facts.statement: The exact placement of fleshy nostrils in Giraffatitan is debated, with researchers hypothesizing as many as five possible locations.
facts.quote: The placement of Giraffatitan nostrils has been the source of much debate with Witmer (2001) describing in Science the hypothesized position of the fleshy nostrils in Giraffatitan in as many as five possible locations.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Giraffatitan possessed a trunk, though the lack of narrow-snouted sauropods tends to discredit this hypothesis.
facts.quote: There has also been the hypothesis of various sauropods, such as Giraffatitan, possessing a trunk. The fact that there were no narrow-snouted sauropods (Giraffatitan included) tends to discredit such a hypothesis.

facts.statement: Teeth wear in Giraffatitan suggests it bit and tore plant matter rather than grinding it, indicating the absence of a trunk.
facts.quote: Stronger evidence for the absence of a trunk is found in the teeth wear of Giraffatitan, which shows the kind of wear that would result from biting and tearing off of plant matter rather than purely grinding, which would be the result of having already ripped the leaves and branches off with a trunk.

facts.statement: The current scientific consensus is that Giraffatitan was a fully terrestrial animal.
facts.quote: The current consensus view, however, is that Giraffatitan was a fully terrestrial animal.

facts.statement: Studies by Lawrence Witmer in 2001 suggest that despite high skull openings, the nostrils of Giraffatitan were located near the tip of the snout.
facts.quote: new studies by Lawrence Witmer (2001) show that, while the nasal openings in the skull were placed high above the eyes, the nostrils would still have been close to the tip of the snout

facts.statement: Glycogen bodies are considered a more likely explanation for the sacral enlargement in Giraffatitan than a 'second brain'.
facts.quote: However, glycogen bodies are a more likely explanation.

facts.statement: In 1929, Janensch assigned Brachiosaurus species to the subfamily Brachiosaurinae within the family Bothrosauropodidae.
facts.quote: In 1929 assigned them to a subfamily Brachiosaurinae within the family Bothrosauropodidae.

facts.statement: In 1997, Salgado proposed that species traditionally considered brachiosaurids were offshoots of the Titanosauriformes stem rather than a separate branch.
facts.quote: In 1997, he published an analysis in which species traditionally considered brachiosaurids were subsequent offshoots of the stem of a larger grouping, the Titanosauriformes, and not a separate branch of their own.

facts.statement: In 2009, Taylor moved Brachiosaurus brancai into its own genus, Giraffatitan, due to noted anatomical differences.
facts.quote: In 2009, Taylor noted multiple anatomical differences between the two Brachiosaurus species, and consequently moved B. brancai into its own genus, Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: Studies from 2012 and 2013 produced conflicting results regarding whether Giraffatitan or Brachiosaurus occupied a more basal position on the evolutionary tree.
facts.quote: A 2012 study by D'Emic placed Giraffatitan in a more basal position, in an earlier branch, than Brachiosaurus, while a 2013 study by Philip Mannion and colleagues had it the other way around.

facts.statement: A 2024 analysis by Han et al. recovered Giraffatitan as the sister taxon to Sonorasaurus within a clade also containing Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: In their 2024 description of Gandititan, Han et al. analyzed the phylogenetic relations of Macronaria, focusing on titanosauriform taxa. They recovered Giraffatitan as the sister taxon to Sonorasaurus, similar to some previous analyses, in a clade also containing Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2001, paleontologist Lawrence M. Witmer rejected the idea that sauropods like Giraffatitan had fleshy nostrils on top of their heads.
facts.quote: The American paleontologist Lawrence M. Witmer rejected this reconstruction in 2001, pointing out that all living vertebrate land animals have their external fleshy nostrils placed at the front of the bony nostril.

facts.statement: Czerkas noted that the location of nostrils in Giraffatitan could not be determined conclusively without skin impressions.
facts.quote: Czerkas speculated on the function of the peculiar brachiosaurid nose, and pointed out that there was no conclusive way to determine where the nostrils where located, unless a head with skin impressions was found.

facts.statement: Some researchers have proposed that Giraffatitan may have had a proboscis to help it reach higher vegetation.
facts.quote: It has been proposed that sauropods, including Giraffatitan, may have had proboscises (trunks) based on the position of the bony narial orifice, to increase their upward reach.

facts.statement: While some studies suggest Giraffatitan lacked a proboscis, the larger facial nerve in this genus leaves the possibility open.
facts.quote: However, Knoll and colleagues also noted that the facial nerve for Giraffatitan was larger, and could therefore not discard the possibility of a proboscis in this genus.

facts.statement: If Giraffatitan were warm-blooded, it would have taken about ten years to reach full size, but if cold-blooded, over 100 years.
facts.quote: If Giraffatitan was endothermic (warm-blooded), it would have taken an estimated ten years to reach full size; if it were instead poikilothermic (cold-blooded), then it would have required over 100 years to reach full size.

facts.statement: If Giraffatitan was warm-blooded, it likely consumed more than 182 kg of food daily.
facts.quote: As a warm-blooded animal, the daily energy demands of Giraffatitan would have been enormous; it would probably have needed to eat more than 182 kg of food per day.

facts.statement: Some scientists propose that large dinosaurs like Giraffatitan were gigantotherms.
facts.quote: Some scientists have proposed that large dinosaurs like Giraffatitan were gigantotherms.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan lived in what is now Tanzania during the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan lived in what is now Tanzania in the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation.

facts.statement: The boundary between the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages is dated at 152.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Since 2012, the boundary between the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian is dated at 152.1 million years ago.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan is the only known species in its genus.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan brancai was a four-legged, herbivorous sauropod with a long neck, relatively short tail, and small brain and skull.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan brancai es un saurópodo de cuatro patas, herbívoro, de cuello largo, una cola relativamente corta y un cerebro y cráneo bastante pequeños.

facts.statement: Unlike other sauropods, Giraffatitan had a giraffe-like build with long front legs compared to its hind legs.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros saurópodos, tenía una constitución similar a la de las actuales jirafas, con largas patas delanteras , en comparación a las traseras.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan had spatulate teeth well-suited for its diet.
facts.quote: Tenía unos dientes espatulados muy adecuados para su dieta.

facts.statement: The skull of Giraffatitan had many holes, likely to reduce weight, and a characteristic crest.
facts.quote: Su cráneo presenta bastantes agujeros, probablemente para reducir su peso, y una cresta característica.

facts.statement: The first toe of its front feet and the first three toes of its hind feet had claws.
facts.quote: En cuanto a sus extremidades, el primer dedo de sus patas delanteras y los tres primeros de sus patas traseras tenían garras.

facts.statement: Based on the holotype specimen HMN SII, Giraffatitan is estimated to have reached a length of 21.8 to 23 meters and a height of 13 meters to the head.
facts.quote: Basándose en el espécimen holotipo, HMN SII, conocido por un esqueleto casi completo que se expone en el Museo de Historia Natural de Berlín, Giraffatitan se estima que alcanzó entre 21,8 y 23 metros de longitud y probablemente medía 13 metros de altura hasta la cabeza.

facts.statement: Recent weight estimates based on reconstructed models accounting for air sacs and muscle mass place Giraffatitan between 23.2 and 39.5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Las estimaciones más recientes de su peso, basadas en modelos reconstruidos que toman en cuenta datos modernos de su osteología, como los sacos de aire y una finamente estimada masa muscular, calculan a este saurópodo en el rango de 23,2 a 39,5 toneladas.

facts.statement: For decades, Giraffatitan was considered the largest known dinosaur worldwide.
facts.quote: Durante décadas, Giraffatitan fue considerado mundialmente como el mayor dinosaurio conocido.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the sauropod Sauroposeidon, known from an incomplete skeleton, likely exceeds the size of Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Más recientemente, se ha descubierto otro saurópodo posiblemente braquiosáurido, Sauroposeidon, basado en un esqueleto incompleto, que parece muy razonable que supere a Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: A second fragmentary specimen, HMN XV2, is known primarily from a hind limb bone, the fibula, which is proportionally 13% larger than that of the holotype.
facts.quote: Se conoce un segundo espécimen fragmentario, HMN XV2, conocido básicamente por un hueso de la extremidad trasera, el peroné, que proporcionalmente es un 13% más grande que el correspondiente al holotipo.

facts.statement: In 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert estimated a weight of 78,258 kilograms for Giraffatitan based on a measured volume of 86.953 cubic meters and an assumed density of 0.9.
facts.quote: En 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert midió un volumen de 86.953 m³. Suponiendo una densidad de 0,9, esto resultó en un peso de 78,258 kilogramos.

facts.statement: In 1980, Dale Alan Russell estimated a much lower weight of 14.8 tonnes for Giraffatitan by extrapolating from the diameter of the humerus and femur.
facts.quote: En 1980, Dale Alan Russell publicó un peso mucho menor de 14,8 toneladas extrapolando el diámetro del húmero y el fémur.

facts.statement: Recent estimates based on reconstructed models using bone volume measurements and accounting for air sac systems and muscle mass range from 23 to 40 tonnes.
facts.quote: Las estimaciones más recientes basadas en modelos reconstruidos a partir de mediciones de volumen óseo, que tienen en cuenta los sistemas extensos de sacos aéreos reductores de peso presentes en los saurópodos, y la masa muscular estimada, están en el rango de 23 a 40 toneladas.

facts.statement: In 2008, Gunga revised the volume estimate to 47.9 cubic meters using more complex geometric shapes.
facts.quote: En 2008, Gunga revisó el volumen, utilizando formas más complejas, a 47,9 m³.

facts.statement: In 2004, Donald Henderson used a computer model to calculate a volume of 32.398 cubic meters and a weight of 25,789 kilograms for Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Donald Henderson en 2004 empleó un modelo de computadora que calculaba un volumen de 32,398 m³ y un peso de 25,789 kilogramos.
